title: Thread-pool starvation: symptoms, tools, fix
summary: Read the counters of a starving service, find the blocked threads with dotnet-stack, and fix the sync-over-async that caused it.

steps.title: What starvation looks like from the outside
body: The on-call alert says: *p99 latency 8 s, CPU 15%, no errors*. Slow but idle is the signature of threads that are **waiting**, not
working. On .NET 9 and later, `dotnet-counters monitor -n Orders` shows the runtime's `System.Runtime` meter. During the incident:
- `thread.count` is **112 on 8 cores** and has been creeping up one or two a second: the pool keeps adding threads because the ones it
- `queue.length` is large: work is queued with no thread free to run it.
- `work_item.count` (completed items, a running total) grows slowly: little is getting done.
- CPU is low: those 112 threads are blocked, not busy.
Healthy, the same service sits at about 8 to 16 threads and a queue near 0. On runtimes before .NET 9 the names are the older

steps.prompt: Another service shows `dotnet.thread_pool.thread.count` = 10 on 8 cores, `queue.length` = 0, CPU 98%, and slow responses. Is this thread-pool starvation?
options: No: the threads are busy computing; this is CPU saturation, so profile the hot code
Yes: raise the minimum thread count
Yes: the queue is empty because the threads are blocked
explain: Starvation is *many threads, low CPU, growing queue*. Few threads at full CPU with an empty queue means the work itself is expensive.
More threads would only add context switches. Reach for `dotnet-trace collect --profile cpu-sampling` or a profiler instead.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: starvation
steps.body: When a .NET service is slow but not busy, these tell you which threads are stuck and where.

toolkit.what: Live runtime metrics: thread count, queue length, completed items, lock contentions, GC.
flags: which meters (comma-separated); System.Runtime is the runtime's own
toolkit.when: first look at a slow service

toolkit.what: Prints the managed stack of every thread, right now. Look for many pool threads stopped in the same wait.
toolkit.when: the problem is happening now and is steady

toolkit.what: Records WaitHandleWait events (.NET 9+) with stacks: every place a thread blocked on .Result, .Wait(), lock or SemaphoreSlim.Wait.
toolkit.when: the stalls come and go; open the .nettrace in PerfView or .NET Events Viewer

toolkit.what: Writes a full memory dump to analyse later (dotnet-dump analyze, Visual Studio Parallel Stacks).
toolkit.when: you must restart the service now but want the evidence

steps.prompt: Match the question to the tool that answers it.
pairs: Is the pool growing and the queue backing up?
Where are the threads stuck right now?
Which call sites block now and then, over 30 seconds?
I must restart; how do I keep the evidence?

steps.title: The stack that gives it away
body: `dotnet-stack report -n Orders` prints hundreds of threads. Most of them end like this (top of the stack first):
- The bottom two frames: this is a **pool** thread.
- `GetResultCore` is `Task<T>.Result`; `SpinThenBlockingWait` is the thread going to sleep on it.
- The first frame of *your* code, `PriceClient.GetPrice`, is the culprit: a synchronous method calling an async one and blocking.
The fix is **async all the way**: `GetPriceAsync` returning `Task<decimal>`, awaited by `HandleAsync`, up to the endpoint.

steps.prompt: The team proposes fixes for the starvation above. Which fix the cause, and which only hide it?
items: Make `GetPrice` async and await it all the way up
Replace the blocking `HttpClient` call with `await client.GetFromJsonAsync(...)`
Add more pods behind the load balancer
explain: Raising the minimum threads makes the pool create blocked threads faster (each one 1 MB of stack and scheduler time); it moves the
cliff, it does not remove it. `Task.Run(...).Result` still blocks the calling thread *and* uses a second one. Scaling out multiplies
the cost. Only removing the synchronous wait gives the thread back.

steps.prompt: Put the incident steps in the order a senior on call would take them.
lines: Confirm the symptom: high latency with low CPU on the dashboards
`dotnet-counters monitor` shows thread count climbing and a long queue
`dotnet-stack report` (or a dump) shows pool threads blocked in `GetResultCore` under `PriceClient.GetPrice`
Mitigate: scale out or restart to buy time, keeping a dump as evidence
Fix: make `GetPrice` async all the way up, then load-test the fix

steps.title: Async all the way, both calls at once
prompt: `SummaryAsync` builds an order summary from two services. It was written in a hurry: it blocks on both calls, one after the other.
2. **starts both calls before awaiting either**, so the waits overlap;
The tests hold both services' answers until both calls have started, so a version that awaits the first before starting the second
never gets its first answer (the tests give up after two seconds).
starter: static Task<string> SummaryAsync(Customers customers, Orders orders, int id)
solution: static async Task<string> SummaryAsync(Customers customers, Orders orders, int id)
template: var dojoTask = SummaryAsync(new Customers(dojoBoth), new Orders(dojoBoth), 3);
Dojo.Check("SummaryAsync returns while the services are still working", !dojoTask.IsCompleted,
"It only returned after the services answered: something blocks the thread.");
Dojo.Check("Both calls are started before either is awaited", dojoDone == dojoTask && dojoBoth.OpenedTogether,
"The services only answer once both calls are in flight. Start both tasks first, then await them.");
if (dojoDone == dojoTask) Dojo.Eq("SummaryAsync(..., 3) gives the summary", "Ada: 5 items", await dojoTask);
class Customers(Both both) { public Task<string> NameAsync(int id) => both.Call("Ada"); }
class Orders(Both both) { public Task<int> CountAsync(int id) => both.Call(5); }

forbid.message: Does not block on a task

hints: Call both methods first and keep the tasks in variables. Await afterwards.
`var a = customers.NameAsync(id); var b = orders.CountAsync(id); await Task.WhenAll(a, b);` then `await a` and `await b` (or `.Result`, safe once they are complete).
explain: Reading `.Result` *after* `await Task.WhenAll(...)` is fine: the tasks are complete, so it does not block. Many teams still prefer
`var name = await nameTask;` for the same effect, because it unwraps exceptions the same way as everywhere else.
